explanations.explanation: Job asks, “How long will you torment me and crush me with your words?” Words, friend. Nobody laid a finger on him, and it still got heavy. I think a long speech can weigh more than a full bag of flour.

Silence isn't what Job is complaining about here. His friends have been talking, and he says they crush him with their words. I bet Job would have taken a little quiet right about now. This time the problem is the speeches.

Nobody is staring a hole in Job in this verse. He says they torment him and crush him with their words. Bildad the Shuhite, one of Job's friends, had just finished a whole speech. That is a lot of talking, and not a single stare is mentioned.

Job says, “Even if I have truly gone astray, my error concerns me alone.” He is telling his friends that even if he did go astray, that's his to carry. I think he's tired of them acting like it's their business. Nothing like a friend who shows up to a mistake with a clipboard.

This one is true, friend. Job really does say it: “Even if I have truly gone astray, my error concerns me alone.” He doesn't say he has gone astray, only that even if he had, it would concern him alone. That little word “if” is doing a lot of work.

Job says, “it is God who has wronged me and drawn His net around me.” Bildad, Job's friend, had been talking about nets that catch the wicked (Job 18:8). Job takes that picture and says the net around him was drawn by God. Notice he says it straight to his friends, and he doesn't hold back.

The Sabeans were raiders who attacked Job's herds (Job 1:15), so it's a fair guess. But Job doesn't mention them here. In this verse he says God drew the net around him. The raiders are not in this speech.

Bildad is the one who brought up nets, so I see why you picked him. Bildad the Shuhite was Job's friend, and he talked about a net catching the wicked (Job 18:8). But Job doesn't say Bildad drew the net around him. He says God did.

explanations.answer: Blocked it so he cannot pass
explanations.explanation: Job says, “He has blocked my way so I cannot pass.” A road that just stops is a hard thing to face. And he adds that God has veiled his paths with darkness. So he can't go forward, and he can't even see where to step.

explanations.answer: Washed it out with a flood
explanations.explanation: A flood would be dramatic, but Job doesn't say that. He says God has blocked his way so he cannot pass. Then he adds that his paths are veiled with darkness. No water anywhere in this verse.

No robbers on this road in the verse. Job says God has blocked his way so he cannot pass. He also says God has veiled his paths with darkness. It's less about who's on the road and more about the road being shut.
Job says God has “removed the crown from my head.” A crown is a sign of honor, and Job says it's gone. Right before that, he says God has stripped him of his honor. It's the same loss, said two ways.
A helmet sounds sturdy, and Job does bring up an army a few verses later. But in this verse, the thing taken off his head is his crown. He's talking about honor, not armor.

I see where you got that. The verse before mentions paths that are veiled with darkness, so the word is close by. But the thing removed from Job's head is his crown. The veil is on the paths, not on him.

Job says, “He uproots my hope like a tree.” A tree pulled out by its roots doesn't just lose a branch, it loses what held it in the ground. That's the picture he picks for his hope. I think this is one of the heaviest lines in the whole speech.
A name feels like something that could be uprooted, but Job doesn't say that. He says God uproots his hope like a tree. His name never comes up in this verse. It's his hope that gets pulled out.
A tree and a harvest go together, so that's a fair guess. Still, Job says God uproots his hope like a tree. He doesn't mention a harvest at all. The thing being pulled up is hope.

This one is false, friend. Job says the opposite: God's anger burns against him, and God “counts me among His enemies.” That's the line to remember. He feels like God has put him on the wrong side of the table.
Right. Job says God's anger burns against him, and that He “counts me among His enemies.” Not friends, enemies. I think this is a heavy verse, so I'll just let it sit.

Job says God's troops “construct a ramp against me and encamp around my tent.” A ramp was built up against a place to get over its defenses. And these troops camp around a tent, which has no walls at all. I bet Job felt like it was a lot of army for one man.

A tower makes sense for an army, but Job says ramp. His troops construct a ramp against him and camp around his tent. A tent with a ramp built against it is a lot of army for one man. I think that's exactly how Job felt.

Gates belong to cities, and Job is sitting in a tent. The verse says the troops construct a ramp against him and camp around his tent. So there is no gate in this picture. Just a ramp and a lot of soldiers.
Job says the opposite. His kinsmen have failed him, and his friends have forgotten him. Everyone who should be near is gone. I think that's a lonely place to be standing.
Right. Job says his kinsmen have failed him and his friends have forgotten him. Nobody is standing by him in this verse. Family and friends, both gone quiet, and I think that stings twice.

Job says, “My guests and maidservants count me as a stranger; I am a foreigner in their sight.” These are people under his own roof, and they look at him like he just walked in off the road. I think that would hurt. He's a stranger in his own house.

Being treated like a king would be nice, friend, but this is the opposite. Job says his guests and maidservants count him as a stranger. He adds that he is a foreigner in their sight. No crown there, since he already said his was removed.

Job doesn't say they see him as a prophet. He says his guests and maidservants count him as a stranger, and a foreigner in their sight. People living in his house look at him like he doesn't belong. That's the sting of it.

Job says, “I call for my servant, but he does not answer, though I implore him with my own mouth.” A man who used to give the orders is now begging. I think the begging part hurts most. He's not even giving a command anymore.
No help comes in this verse. Job calls for his servant, and the servant does not answer. Job even implores him with his own mouth. The servant gives no response at all.

Nobody is calling the elders. Job says he calls for his servant and the servant does not answer, though Job implores him with his own mouth. There's no running around in this verse. Just a call with no reply.

Job says, “Even little boys scorn me; when I appear, they deride me.” The word “even” is the sting. If the youngest ones in town are doing it, it must feel like everybody is. I think that's why he says it this way.

Merchants just passing through don't show up in this verse. Job says even little boys scorn him, and when he appears they deride him. The word “even” points to people you'd least expect. It's the little boys.
You'd expect elders to be hard on a man, but they aren't named here. Job says even little boys scorn him, and when he appears they deride him. That's why he says “even.” It's the little boys.

Job says, “All my best friends despise me, and those I love have turned against me.” That is two blows in one verse. Best friends and loved ones, both. I think it's one of the loneliest lines in his speech.
This one is true, friend. Job says, “All my best friends despise me, and those I love have turned against me.” He really does say it. It's one of the sad notes in a speech that has a lot of them.
Job says, “Have pity on me, my friends, have pity.” He says it twice, like a man who's run out of other ways to ask. He doesn't ask them to fix anything. I think he just wants them to be gentle.
Silence would have been a fair thing to ask for, but that's not what he begs for. Job says, “Have pity on me, my friends, have pity.” Same word, said twice. It's pity he's after.

His friends have already given him plenty of advice, and Job doesn't ask for more. He says, “Have pity on me, my friends, have pity.” Pity, twice. I think he wanted a soft landing more than another opinion.

Job asks, “Why do you persecute me as God does? Will you never get enough of my flesh?” Right before it, he says the hand of God has struck him. Now he asks why they pile on too. I think he can't see why they'd add to it.

Job really does ask this, friend. He says, “Why do you persecute me as God does? Will you never get enough of my flesh?” It comes right after he says the hand of God has struck him. So the question is aimed at his friends.

Job wants his words written with an iron stylus on lead, “or chiseled in stone forever.” That's the hardest and longest-lasting writing he can think of. Whatever he has to say, he wants it to stay. Anything in stone doesn't wash away.
Sand is the first thing the tide takes. Job wants his words to last, so he says “chiseled in stone forever.” The iron stylus on lead is in the same line. Nothing he names here would blow away.
Wax wouldn't last a day in my ovens. Job asks for something that lasts: an iron stylus on lead, or “chiseled in stone forever.” He wants his words to stay put. Stone is the one that fits.

Job says, “But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth.” After all those heavy verses, that “But” is a turn. Everything around him is falling apart, and he still says “I know.” That's the verse people have held onto for a long time.
Job doesn't say a word about his riches coming back. What he says he knows is “that my Redeemer lives.” He looks past what he lost. The hope he names is a Person, and not a bank account.

That sounds hopeful, but Job doesn't say it here. He says, “I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth.” He doesn't promise himself healing. What he holds onto is that his Redeemer lives.

Job says, “Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God.” He's looking straight at what has happened to his body, and he doesn't look away. And then comes the “yet.” Skin goes, but the seeing stays.
Job says, “yet in my flesh I will see God.” That's the whole hope in four words. He doesn't say he'll see an answer or a reason. He says he'll see God Himself.
A house is something Job could lose, but it's not the word in this verse. He says, “Even after my skin has been destroyed.” So the thing named is his skin. His house is not mentioned here.

Wealth isn't what Job is talking about here. The verse says, “Even after my skin has been destroyed, yet in my flesh I will see God.” The thing destroyed is his skin, and the thing he hopes for is God. Nothing in this verse is about money.
Angels aren't in this verse at all, friend. Job says, “yet in my flesh I will see God.” He doesn't ask for messengers. It's God Himself he says he'll see.
Job says the opposite. He says, “I will see Him for myself; my eyes will behold Him, and not as a stranger.” No middleman, no report passed along. He says his own eyes will see Him.
Right. Job says, “I will see Him for myself; my eyes will behold Him, and not as a stranger.” That's “for myself” and “my eyes.” He isn't waiting for someone to bring him the news.

Job tells his friends, “then you should fear the sword yourselves, because wrath brings punishment by the sword, so that you may know there is a judgment.” He turns his friends' warnings around on them. I think a man who has been blamed this long can finally say something back.
A whirlwind isn't in this speech. Job warns his friends to “fear the sword yourselves.” He says wrath brings punishment by the sword. The word he uses is sword.

A plague isn't what Job names. He says, “you should fear the sword yourselves, because wrath brings punishment by the sword.” He ends with a warning that there is a judgment. The thing he points them to is the sword.
